title: Best Stretch to Stay Calm
statement:
A café is open for n minutes. In minute i, customers[i] people are served. The clerk is in a bad mood in minute i when moody[i] = 1; everyone served in such a minute leaves unhappy. In the other minutes everyone leaves happy.

The clerk can pull themselves together once, for exactly k consecutive minutes, and is not moody during that stretch. Return the largest possible number of happy customers over the whole day.

examples.why: 11 people are happy anyway. Calming minutes 4 and 5 wins back 1 + 3 = 4. The busy minute 3 is already happy, so covering it gains nothing.
The two moody minutes are not next to each other, so one stretch of 2 minutes wins back only one of the 5s.
The stretch covers the whole day.

hints: Split the answer into two parts: the customers who are happy no matter what, and the extra ones the calm stretch wins back.
The first part is fixed. The second part is the sum of customers[i] over moody minutes inside a window of length k. Which window maximizes it?
Slide a window of length k: add the minute that enters if it is moody, subtract the minute that leaves if it was moody, and track the best sum.

explain.intuition:
Minutes where the clerk is fine are happy whatever you do, so count them once and forget them. What the calm stretch changes is only the moody minutes it covers: it wins back exactly the customers of those minutes. So the question becomes "which window of length k contains the most customers in moody minutes?"

That is a fixed-size sliding window. Moving the window one minute to the right adds one minute and removes one, so the window total updates in O(1) instead of being summed again. It is the same as a rolling "last k minutes" counter on a dashboard.
steps: Compute gain = sum of customers[i] · moody[i] for the first k minutes; set best = gain.
For i from k to n − 1: add customers[i] · moody[i], subtract customers[i − k] · moody[i − k], update best.
pitfalls: Counting all customers inside the window as the gain. Minutes that were already happy would be counted twice; the first example would put the window on the 7.
Picking the k moody minutes with the most customers. They must be consecutive, as the second example shows.
Off-by-one when sliding: the minute that leaves is i − k, not i − k + 1.

solutions.title: Try every window
solutions.idea: For each start, add up what the calm stretch wins back by scanning its k minutes.

solutions.title: Fixed-size sliding window
solutions.idea: The gain of a window changes by one minute in and one minute out as it slides.

followups: The clerk can calm down twice, each time for k minutes, and the stretches may not overlap. How do prefix and suffix bests help?
Return the start minute of the best stretch; on ties, the earliest.
